sections.heading: A.1 Literature Review
sections.text: Table 5: Overview of the 70 sycophancy papers we reviewed for deriving the taxonomy. Sorted alphabetically by first author. Cells column maps each paper to the taxonomy cells it covers. Abbreviations: Pos = Position, Per = Person, V = Verifiable, S = Subjective, T = Traits, Em = Emotions, E = Explicit, I = Implicit. ‘—’ indicates the paper did not operationalize a specific cell. Citation Definition & Operationalization Setting Main Contribution Cells Arvin 2025 Tendency of LLMs to agree with or defer to user suggestions even when incorrect. Operationalized as accuracy changes when students hint at a correct vs. incorrect answer, flip rate toward the user-suggested option, and token-level probability shifts. Educational; MMLU MC in simulated student–LLM interaction. Introduces ecologically valid educational prompting; subtle student hints substantially bias model accuracy, with implications for educational equity. Pos-V/E Asher et al. 2026 “Statistical sycophancy”: tendency to inflate results or engage in specification search when prompted toward significance. Operationalized via a 2 × \times 4 factorial varying research framing and significance pressure; sycophancy evidenced by movement toward larger/more significant estimates and explicit specification search. Statistical analysis / coding agents; 4 political-science papers (SOO, RDD, DiD, RCT). Extends sycophancy to statistical reasoning; standard prompting mostly stable, but a “nuclear” uncertainty-reporting prompt bypasses guardrails and induces systematic specification search in analytically flexible designs. Pos-V/E; Pos-V/I Rrv et al. 2024 Model aligns responses to user intent even when misleading, generating factually incorrect statements from misleading keyword sets. Operationalized as sycophantic factual statement generation under generic and domain-specific prompts, and reduction under four mitigation strategies. Factual generation; 5 domain-specific prompts (Entertainment, Broadcast, History, Science, Legal). Introduces a misleading-keyword paradigm; LLMs can be pulled into factual error without explicit user opinions; evaluates practical mitigation defenses. Pos-V/E Atwell et al. 2025 Overly agreeable behavior where models excessively align with user views, affirming assumptions rather than providing independent reasoning. Operationalized as residual belief shift after controlling for rational evidence, compared across Abstract, Third-Party, and User conditions; descriptive (residual social bias) and normative (deviation from Bayesian-consistent posterior) metrics. Subjective/uncertain reasoning; moral judgment, cultural acceptability, forecasting. Separates sycophancy from rational belief updating via residual social bias; enables label-free evaluation through Bayesian consistency in subjective domains. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I Barkett et al. 2025 Models agree with user beliefs instead of being truthful; sycophantic tendencies linked to truth-bias asymmetry. Operationalized as asymmetry between truth accuracy and deception accuracy in veracity judgment tasks. Veracity detection; truthful vs. deceptive hotel reviews. Links truth-bias to sycophantic tendencies; capability gains do not fully resolve models’ tendency to err toward acceptance. Pos-V/E Batista and Griffiths 2026 Tendency to generate responses aligned with user’s beliefs; formally, biased sampling conditional on the user’s current hypothesis rather than the true data-generating distribution. Operationalized in a modified Wason 2-4-6 task comparing sycophantic vs. unbiased AI agents; sycophancy evidenced by suppressed discovery and inflated confidence. Hypothesis testing / multi-turn; Wason rule discovery, N = 557 N{=}557 . Shows sycophantic AI misleads even rational Bayesian agents by biasing the evidence stream; reframes sycophancy as a sampling distortion mechanism. Pos-V/I Batzner et al. 2025 Tendency to agree with or reinforce user-provided information even when incorrect. Operationalized as agreement with incorrect user answers and answer changes under user suggestion in political-QA settings. Factual QA / political alignment; German-parties benchmark. Shows sycophancy arises from reasoning failure under user influence and can be mitigated by improving reasoning; reframes sycophancy as a reasoning rather than preference-alignment issue. Pos-S/E Beigi et al. 2025 Tendency to agree with incorrect user information; also blind conformity without critical reasoning. Operationalized as two types: Type-1 (retracting correct answers under challenge) and Type-2 (incorporating user errors despite correct knowledge); truthfulness accuracy under misleading inputs on SycophancyEval. Factual QA / challenge prompts. Introduces SMART; reframes mitigation from output editing to reasoning optimization; uncertainty-aware trajectory optimization reduces both sycophancy types while preserving OOD performance. Pos-V/E Bo et al. 2025 Excessive enthusiasm, agreement, and flattery; models avoid contradicting users with incorrect beliefs, reflecting the user’s mental model irrespective of correctness. Operationalized via downstream effects on mental model accuracy, reliance on incorrect suggestions, and task performance in high vs. low sycophancy conditions. Technical problem solving / coding; 24 novice participants performing machine learning debugging tasks. Demonstrates sycophancy as an “invisible” failure mode: models reinforce misconceptions, increase over-reliance, and degrade performance while remaining polite. Pos-V/E; Per-T/E Carro 2024 Tendency to align outputs with user’s perceived preferences, beliefs, or opinions to appear favorable regardless of factual correctness. Operationalized as trust measured via continued-use behavior and self-reported trust/perceived usefulness after exposure to a sycophantic vs. standard GPT. Factual QA; ground-truth questions with model assistance. Shows sycophantic behavior reduces rather than increases user trust in a factual task setting. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Per-T/E Çelebi et al. 2025 Excessive conformity; tendency to align with, validate, or flatter user views even when doing so reduces factual accuracy or epistemic integrity. Operationalized as accuracy degradation under authority-injected false claims, follow rate, confidence shifts via log-likelihood calibration, and an 8-state behavioral taxonomy. Factual MC QA; 1,302 MMLU-style questions across 13 domains. Introduces PARROT, a robustness benchmark measuring not only answer switching but also confidence inversion/epistemic collapse; reveals large robustness differences across models and domains. Pos-V/E Chandra et al. 2026 Chatbot biased toward messages that appease users, selecting user-validating evidence rather than impartial evidence. Operationalized as per-round sycophancy rate π \pi ; catastrophic delusional spiraling defined as posterior P ⁡ ( H = 0 ) > 99 % P(H{=}0){>}99\% in a Bayesian conversational model. Multi-turn belief updating; binary world-state hypothesis evaluation. Formally links chatbot sycophancy to delusional spiraling; shows even ideal Bayesian users remain vulnerable, and “factual” sycophants still carry nonzero spiraling risk. Pos-V/I; Pos-S/I Chang 2025 Prioritizing agreeableness over correctness; specifically trace-output inconsistency: model derives one answer internally but outputs another to please users. Operationalized as the Final Output Gap (correct reasoning precedes sycophantic output) and sycophancy rate under adversarial authority hints on CAP-GSM8K. Math reasoning; CAP-GSM8K with adversarial authority hints; OOD on ARC-AGI. Reframes sycophancy as a control failure; identifies Inverse Scaling and Final Output Gap missed by outcome evaluation; proposes ground-truth-free inference-time process verifier (RCA). Pos-V/E Chen et al. 2025a Models produce answers catering to user expectations rather than truthful responses; mirror user suggestions rather than what they would produce unbiased. Operationalized as performance on Answer Suggestion and Are You Sure tasks, measuring whether the model accepts correct vs. rejects incorrect suggestions. Factual QA; suggestion-conditioned prompts and challenge tasks. Demonstrates that alignment amplifies sycophancy in open-source models; proposes Self-Augmented Preference Alignment reframing the task as suggestion assessment rather than following. Pos-V/E Chen et al. 2025b Excessive agreeableness, treated as a persona-like trait that can be induced, monitored, and suppressed through activation-space control. Operationalized as a sycophancy score (0–100) from an automated evaluation prompt and as movement along a learned persona vector. Open-ended conversational / persona control. Recasts sycophancy as a latent direction in activation space; shows it can be monitored, predicted, and controlled at deployment and during fine-tuning. — Chen et al. 2025c Excessive agreement with users at the expense of accuracy; specifically aligning with an incorrect implied belief and generating false information despite knowing the premise is false. Operationalized as compliance with illogical medical requests and failure to reject misinformation prompts involving equivalent drugs. Medical / factual; brand–generic drug pairs and illogical comparative requests. Shows medical sycophancy arises from over-helpfulness even when the model knows the premise is false; demonstrates practical mitigation strategies. Pos-V/E Chen et al. 2024 Tendency to prioritize adherence to user prompts over truthful responses; admits mistakes despite initially correct answers. Operationalized as accuracy change and answer switching after “Are you sure?” challenge on SycophancyEval. Factual QA / multi-turn; SycophancyEval (MMLU, TruthfulQA). Identifies specific attention heads responsible for sycophantic behavior; targeted pinpoint fine-tuning reduces sycophancy while preserving general performance. Pos-V/E Cheng et al. 2026b Agreeing with and flattering users at the cost of correctness; social sycophancy as excessive preservation of user’s face (desired self-image). Operationalized across four behavioral dimensions: validation, indirectness, acceptance of flawed framing, and moral affirmation. Social / advice / moral; general advice queries and r/AITA moral dilemmas. Expands sycophancy beyond belief agreement to face-preservation and implicit alignment; shows models systematically validate users’ self-image. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-Em/E; Per-Em/I Cheng et al. 2026a AI excessively agreeing with or flattering users; specifically “social sycophancy” affirming the user’s actions, perspectives, and self-image. Operationalized as action endorsement rate across open-ended advice and interpersonal-conflict datasets, including endorsement of harmful actions. Social / advice / interpersonal conflict; AITA-style dilemmas, live interaction. Introduces and validates social sycophancy as broader than belief agreement; shows harmful downstream effects on conflict repair intentions, trust, and dependence. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-Em/E; Per-Em/I Christian and Mazor 2026 User-serving bias where models find it hard to “un-know” biasing information about user identity, assigning excess weight to the user’s interests. Operationalized as logit-difference in responses when party is “me” vs. “them” across 60 counterbalanced dispute scenarios. Subjective / interpersonal dispute judgments; user vs. other fairness decisions. Reframes sycophancy as failure of counterfactual self-simulation; shows that prompting models to ignore user identity is unreliable, while truly blinded outputs dramatically reduce sycophancy. Pos-S/I Denison et al. 2024 Simple specification gaming: model produces outputs conforming to user biases. Operationalized as outputs matching user’s implied political views and ratings scored as sycophantic by a grader model in gameable environments. Subjective / social; political sycophancy and tool-use flattery. Connects sycophancy to broader specification gaming; shows generalization from early sycophancy/flattery settings to later reward-tampering. Pos-S/E; Per-T/E Du et al. 2025 Excessive and/or uncritical validation, amplification, or alignment with user assertions—factual, cognitive, or affective. Operationalized as three types: informational (agreement with false claims), cognitive (uncritical alignment with beliefs/evaluations), and affective (mirroring emotional states). Conceptual / cross-context; not tied to one benchmark. Reframes sycophancy as a communicative construct; introduces tripartite typology with two interactional dimensions (personalization, critical prompting) and proposes the AISPM as a unifying theory. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Pos-V/I; Pos-S/I; Per-T/E; Per-Em/E; Per-T/I; Per-Em/I Dubois et al. 2026 Tendency to favour user-affirming responses (agreement, validation, flattery) over critical engagement. Operationalized via rubric-based scoring of five facets: excessive agreement, flattery, avoiding disagreement, user-preference alignment, and validation seeking, comparing question vs. non-question framing. Subjective / advice-like; single-turn prompts across hobbies, relationships, mental health, and medical topics. Shows causally that input framing drives sycophancy: non-questions, stronger epistemic certainty, and first-person framing increase it; rewriting as questions reduces sycophancy more than “don’t be sycophantic” instructions. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-T/E; Per-Em/E Fanous et al. 2025 Tendency to prioritize user agreement over independent reasoning, sacrificing truthfulness. Operationalized as progressive sycophancy (agreement leads to correct answer) vs. regressive sycophancy (agreement leads to incorrect answer) under preemptive vs. in-context rebuttal conditions. Factual + domain-specific; mathematics (AMPS) and medical advice (MedQuad). Introduces SycEval; shows sycophancy is common, persistent, and sensitive to interaction structure; distinguishes beneficial from harmful forms. Pos-V/E Gao and Zhang 2025 Models generate biased responses reflecting user beliefs rather than facts; overly catering to users and endorsing human errors. Operationalized as Consistency Transformation Rate (CTR) and Error Introduction Rate (EIR) after incorrect human feedback in multi-round dialogue. Multimodal / VLM; multi-turn; object existence, art style, driving behavior reasoning. Introduces SyEval-VL; extends sycophancy to VLMs; proposes retrieval-based mitigation (HFRAG) triggered by user disagreement. Pos-V/E Genadi et al. 2026 Model tendency to align with user opinions at the expense of factual accuracy; specifically correct → \rightarrow incorrect sycophancy after user challenge. Operationalized as sycophancy rate (proportion of initially correct answers changed to incorrect after challenge) and linear probe accuracy on internal activations. Factual QA / multi-turn; TruthfulQA with “are you sure?” follow-ups. Identifies a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads as the strongest steerable locus of sycophancy; simple linear steering reduces correct → \rightarrow incorrect reversals. Pos-V/E Guo 2024 Deceptive behavior in which a model tailors responses to match the user’s preferred answer rather than being truthful. Operationalized via political/ideological mirroring, ethical mirroring, and education-based sandbagging across subjective prompts. Subjective / political, ethical, and educational contexts. Places sycophancy inside a broader taxonomy of AI deception alongside strategic deception, imitation, and unfaithful reasoning. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I Hong et al. 2025 Conforming to user beliefs regardless of factual accuracy or ethical soundness. Operationalized as Turn of Flip (how quickly a model conforms) and Number of Flip (how frequently it shifts stance) under sustained user pressure. Multi-turn / free-form conversational; 3 real-world scenarios. Introduces SYCON Bench; extends evaluation from single-turn correctness to multi-turn dialogue dynamics across 17 LLMs. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E Huang et al. 2025 User-appeasing behaviors where models provide misleading information to gain favor or comply with perceived user expectations. Operationalized as deception rate scored on both internal thought and final response across single-turn and multi-turn user-assistant settings. Cross-domain; Economy, Healthcare, Education, Social Interaction, Entertainment. Establishes DeceptionBench with sycophancy as one intrinsic driver; shows user-appeasing tendencies intensify under reward, pressure, and iterative feedback. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E Irpan et al. 2025 Models adopt user beliefs or are hijacked by user opinions; sycophancy as sensitivity to irrelevant sycophantic prompt cues. Operationalized as deviation between responses to semantically equivalent prompts when one includes sycophantic cues, framing failure as a consistency violation. Factual QA / MMLU-style; single-turn prompt transformations. Reframes sycophancy as a consistency failure; introduces self-supervised consistency training that enforces prompt-cue invariance without labeled datasets. Pos-V/E; Pos-V/I Jain et al. 2026 A broad class of mirroring behaviors; specifically agreement sycophancy (overly affirmative responses) and perspective sycophancy (reflecting user’s viewpoint). Operationalized via LLM-judge agreement scoring and participant Likert ratings across zero-shot, synthetic, user-history, and memory-profile context types. Personal advice + political explanation; long-context; 2 weeks of real interaction data from 38 users. Shows sycophancy is interaction-dependent, not a fixed model property; long-context user data and memory profiles often increase sycophancy. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-Em/E Kaur 2025 Tendency to align outputs with user’s stated belief; models alter responses to mirror the stance expressed by the user. Operationalized as stance shift magnitude, directional agreement rate, flip score, and consistency across repeated argumentative runs. Political / subjective; Political Compass Test propositions with GPT-4-generated arguments. Shows explicit argumentation induces sycophancy; models become stance-fickle, shifting or reversing positions to mirror arguments, with stronger arguments producing stronger effects. Pos-S/E Kelley and Riedl 2026 Excessive conformity to user beliefs including biased validation; distinguishes affective alignment (validation, tone) from epistemic alignment (belief adoption, resistance to influence). Operationalized as flip rate under rebuttals, framing shifts in AITA scenarios, and openness under agreement/challenge across 9 LLMs. Social / subjective / multi-turn; advice, moral judgment, debate, goal alignment, rebuttal tasks. Introduces a two-dimensional affective vs. epistemic framework; shows personalization systematically increases affective sycophancy while having role-dependent effects on epistemic independence. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-Em/E; Per-Em/I Khan et al. 2024 Models adjust responses to align with human perspective even without objective correctness; distinguishes preference-driven and persona-based sycophancy. Operationalized via paired sycophantic vs. non-sycophantic responses across preference-conditioned and identity-conditioned prompts. Subjective / social; preference-conditioned and persona/identity-conditioned prompts. Introduces a DPO-based mitigation approach and dedicated dataset targeting both preference-driven and persona-based sycophancy. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I Kim and Khashabi 2025 Models generate responses aligning with user’s stated belief; specifically models endorse user counterarguments or defer to the user in follow-up turns. Operationalized as rate of accepting the user’s counterargument, comparing conversational vs. evaluative/judge framing of identical content. Factual / multi-turn QA; CommonsenseQA, LogiQA, MedMCQA, MMLU, MMLU-Pro. Shows sycophancy is strongly shaped by interaction framing; models more likely to endorse conflicting content as a user follow-up than when both options are presented simultaneously. Pos-V/E Kim et al. 2026 Tendency to conform to user beliefs rather than factual information. Operationalized as stance flipping under pushback, Turn of Flip (ToF), Resistance (proportion maintaining original stance per turn), and Sticky Incorrect Ratio (SIR). Medical / multi-turn; MedCaseReasoning and PubMedQA with escalatory pushback. Introduces Resistance as a turn-level metric; shows models abandon correct answers more readily than incorrect ones under user pressure. Pos-V/E Kran et al. 2025 Chatbot displays slight dishonesty to reinforce user’s echo chambers and filter bubbles. Operationalized as frequency of reinforcing user beliefs in adversarial prompts within the DarkBench category set across 14 LLMs. Subjective / adversarial conversational; sycophancy as one of six dark patterns. Places sycophancy inside a dark-patterns framework; benchmarks how often major chatbots reinforce user echo chambers. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I Kwik 2025 Model outputs conform to user’s views even if incorrect; responding to subtle challenge prompts and inferring preferences from interaction history. Operationalized as responses conforming to explicit/implicit user beliefs in military decision-support scenarios. Military / decision-support / high-stakes planning. Extends sycophancy to military AI; argues it aggravates confirmation bias and induces long-term organizational overtrust; calls for user training to complement technical mitigation. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I Laban et al. 2023 Tendency to change answers in response to user challenge, causing deterioration of accuracy between first and final prediction. Operationalized as flip rate and the FlipFlop effect (accuracy drop between initial and final predictions after “Are you sure?”). Factual / multi-turn classification. Introduces the standardized FlipFlop evaluation; demonstrates widespread accuracy-degrading answer-switching across models. Pos-V/E Li et al. 2025 Prevalent hallucination where models blindly agree with users’ opinions even when incorrect or malicious. Operationalized via the MM-SY benchmark, with analysis of attention distributions to image tokens in sycophantic vs. non-sycophantic cases. Multimodal / VLM; visual language models. First dedicated extension of sycophancy evaluation to VLMs; introduces MM-SY; shows high-layer image attention is implicated in resisting or enabling sycophancy. Pos-V/E Liu et al. 2025 Tendency to excessively agree with or flatter users at the expense of factual accuracy; behavior that generates responses to satisfy users. Operationalized as Feedback, Are You Sure, Answer, and Mimicry sycophancy subtypes, tracking progressive factual degradation over 1, 3, and 7 turns. Factual / multi-turn; TruthfulQA and MMLU-Pro. Introduces TRUTH DECAY benchmark; shows sycophancy compounds over conversation in ways single-turn tests fail to capture. Pos-V/E; Pos-V/I Malmqvist 2025 Excessively agreeing with or flattering users. Operationalized via agreement and flattery behaviors across prior studies and evaluation of mitigation approaches. Cross-setting survey; no original task. Technical survey organizing prior work on causes, impacts, measurement, and mitigation of sycophancy. — Natan and Tsur 2026 Conversational dynamic in which models repeat and validate user views or retract correct answers under pressure; sycophancy serves the user at explicit cost to another party. Operationalized as deviation from the correct answer in zero-sum factual bet prompts, comparing user-vs-friend against neutral two-friends framing. Factual QA / zero-sum bets; 100 TruthfulQA questions rewritten as bets. Introduces a direct, neutral, zero-sum evaluation; all models are biased but not all are sycophantic; identifies interaction with recency bias and “moral remorse” overcompensation. Pos-V/E; Pos-V/I Noshin et al. 2026 Tendency to align outputs with users’ perceived preferences at the expense of accuracy; manifests as affirming incorrect claims, mirroring biases, or offering excessive praise. Operationalized via user-reported detection in Reddit discussions and an DCR (Detection-Categorization–Response) epistemological framework. Conversational / real-world; Reddit discussions of ChatGPT interactions. Shifts literature from model-centric to user-centered perspective; shows users detect, categorize, and respond to sycophancy; argues it is context-dependent rather than universally harmful. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Pos-V/I; Pos-S/I; Per-T/E; Per-Em/E Pandey et al. 2025 Tendency to prioritize user agreement, emotional validation, or social compliance over principled reasoning; latent bias manifesting as preference for agreeableness. Operationalized via forced-choice preference for a sycophantic vs. principled response across 420 hand-curated prompts, with cluster-specific activation steering. Single-turn / social / subjective; five thematic domains (societal, personal, interpersonal, creative, belief). Introduces Beacon forced-choice paradigm; shows sycophancy decomposes into distinct linguistic and affective sub-biases that can be selectively mitigated. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-Em/E; Per-Em/I Papadatos and Freedman 2024 LLMs prioritize agreement with users over accurate statements, disproportionately agreeing even on objectively false content. Operationalized as feedback sycophancy on poem evaluations: like/dislike feedback positivity and positivity gap, classified via linear probes on reward-model activations. Social / evaluative; poem evaluation conditioned on user’s stated liking. Introduces a reward-model probing method that penalizes sycophancy; shows it can reduce feedback sycophancy during Best-of-N optimization. Pos-S/E; Per-T/E Park et al. 2024 Subtype of AI deception: models tailor responses to match the user’s preferred answer regardless of accuracy. Operationalized via political/ideological alignment and ethical mirroring in persona-conditioned interactions. Political / ethical / persona-conditioned. Places sycophancy within a broader taxonomy of AI deception; distinguishes it from strategic deception and imitation. Pos-S/E Peng et al. 2026 Tendency to align with user preferences rather than objective standards; specifically the risk of acquiescing to patient pressure for inappropriate care. Operationalized as acquiescence rate under five adversarial persuasion tactics across three Choosing Wisely clinical scenarios. Medical / multi-turn clinical; simulated ER encounters with adversarial patients. Introduces SycoEval-EM; shows static medical benchmarks do not predict robustness to social pressure; acquiescence varies widely across 20 LLMs. Pos-V/E Perez et al. 2023 LLMs tailor responses to match a user’s preferred answer or align with their stated view rather than providing independent responses. Operationalized as matching user’s stated political affiliation, agreeing with user’s philosophical view, or repeating user’s preferred answer in subjective QA. Subjective / political and philosophical opinion tasks. Introduces scalable evaluation of sycophancy using model-written evaluations; shows it emerges systematically in RLHF-trained models. Pos-S/E Petrov et al. 2025 Tendency to uncritically accept incorrect user statements as facts. Operationalized as the rate of producing a convincing but flawed proof for a false statement, judged on a scale from fully sycophantic to ideal. Math theorem proving; false-but-well-posed competition problems. Introduces BrokenMath; sycophancy is widespread, stronger in proof-based than final-answer tasks, and increases with problem difficulty. Pos-V/E Pi et al. 2025 MLLMs agree with the user regardless of factual accuracy; sycophantic modality gap: behavior is significantly more prominent with image than text inputs. Operationalized as flip rate after user opinion injection; resistance to misleading vs. responsiveness to corrective instructions in two-round dialogue. Multimodal / visual QA; image vs. text-input comparison. Identifies the sycophantic modality gap; proposes Sycophantic Reflective Tuning (SRT) to reduce misleading compliance without excess stubbornness. Pos-V/E Pitre et al. 2025 Agents agreeing with each other rather than critically evaluating perspectives; mimicking another agent’s answer without independent reasoning. Operationalized as sycophancy percentage (instances of answer copying), fast inaccurate consensus, and cyclic sycophancy across six reasoning benchmarks. Multi-agent debate; KITAB, CLUTRR, HotpotQA, Ethics, TriviaQA, GSM8K. First systematic study of sycophancy in multi-agent LLM systems; CONSENSAGENT reduces sycophancy by 7–30% while improving consensus speed and accuracy. Pos-V/E Rabby et al. 2026 Inclination to align with user’s stated/implied opinion even when it contradicts factual or ethical reasoning; moral sycophancy as breakdown of ethical consistency under user influence. Operationalized as follow-up responses becoming morally incorrect after user disagreement, with asymmetric Error Introduction Rate (EIR) vs. Error Correction Rate (ECR). Multimodal / moral judgment; Moralise and M3oralBench image-based tasks. Introduces moral sycophancy as a distinct multimodal failure mode; user disagreement produces consistent asymmetry toward morally worse follow-up judgments. Pos-S/E Rahman et al. 2025 Excessive tendency to agree with user input at the expense of factual accuracy or in contradiction of visual evidence. Operationalized via comparison of base vs. positively and negatively influenced prompts in PENDULUM; conformance to user suggestion vs. image evidence. Multimodal / VQA; ≈ \approx 2,000 human-curated pairs across 6 image domains. Introduces PENDULUM; MLLMs can prioritize user agreement over visual evidence; robustness varies substantially by model and image domain. Pos-V/E Ranaldi and Pucci 2023 Models align answers to a perceived user view at the cost of accuracy; changing an answer when challenged by a user. Operationalized as the FlipFlop effect: accuracy deterioration and flipping probabilities after “Are you sure?”-style challenges. Factual / multi-turn classification. Introduces a standardized multi-turn framework for measuring answer-switching; behavior is widespread and accuracy-degrading across models. Pos-V/E Ranaldi and Pucci 2026 Tendency to align with user-implied beliefs even when these conflict with correctness, uncertainty, or logical reasoning. Operationalized as binary alignment score (sync) measuring endorsement of user-implied target, with SYCpre/SYCpost and Sycophancy Mitigation Rate (SMR). Mixed; factual MC QA, open-ended QA, multilingual (11 languages), multi-turn. Reframes sycophancy as a policy-level failure of agreement control; agentic control reduces sycophancy while preserving performance across tasks, models, and languages. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E Rathje et al. 2025 Excessively agreeable and validating; chatbots that validate rather than challenge users’ pre-existing beliefs via one-sided fact presentation. Operationalized as downstream attitude extremity, certainty, perceived lack of bias, and preference to re-engage, contrasting sycophantic vs. disagreeable chatbots. Subjective / political / multi-turn; 3 preregistered experiments ( n = 3,285 n{=}3{,}285 ). Shows people prefer sycophantic chatbots; brief interactions increase attitude extremity and overconfidence; effects driven mainly by one-sided facts rather than validation alone. Pos-S/E; Pos-S/I; Per-T/E; Per-Em/E Rehani et al. 2026 Tendency to overly agree with and flatter users; in social contexts, flattering and validating rather than informing. Operationalized via the Social Sycophancy Scale: a 3-factor validated instrument (Uncritical Agreement, Obsequiousness, Excitement) applied by human and LLM raters. Social / subjective / moral; no ground-truth contexts. Introduces the first psychometrically validated scale for measuring social sycophancy without ground truth; perceived sycophancy is multidimensional and multivalent. Pos-S/E; Per-T/E; Per-Em/E Richter et al. 2025 Tendency to align with implicit misconceptions in user-like questions rather than highlight or dispute them. Operationalized as error rates for plain user-like questions vs. prompts to “base answer on scientific evidence” or “explicitly correct unsupported assumptions” on neuromyth tasks. Educational / misconception correction; isolated neuromyth classification vs. applied educator-style questions. Sharp gap between isolated misconception detection and applied use: LLMs outperform humans on direct identification but fail to challenge misconceptions in applied questions; corrective prompts substantially reduce this. Pos-V/I Shapira et al. 2026 Tendency to affirm a user’s stated or implied stance even when it conflicts with factual accuracy; formally, endorsing a user’s false belief when the prompt signals it. Operationalized as a formal statistic for agreement with false implied stances and empirical measurement of reward gaps between sycophantic vs. non-sycophantic responses. General prompt-response; factual and stance-laden prompts including multi-turn histories. Provides a causal mechanism for why RLHF increases sycophancy; derives a principled training-time correction (minimal agreement penalty). Pos-V/E; Pos-V/I Sharma et al. 2024 Tendency to generate responses matching user beliefs over truthful ones, prioritizing alignment with user views even at the cost of correctness. Operationalized across three types: answer sycophancy (revising under challenge), feedback sycophancy (biased quality evaluation), and mimicry sycophancy (repeating user errors). Factual (math, geography, trivia), subjective (politics, opinions), feedback (arguments, poems). Introduces a multi-dimensional empirical framework demonstrating sycophancy as a general behavior across task types; links it to RLHF. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Pos-V/I; Per-T/E Sicilia et al. 2025 Proclivity to agree with users even when wrong; bias propagating from answers into externalized uncertainty estimates. Operationalized as answer and uncertainty changes with vs. without user suggestions, compared across user correctness and confidence levels. Factual QA and dialogue-based collaborative prediction; BBH, MMLU-Pro, conversation forecasting. Shows sycophancy affects uncertainty estimates as well as answers; introduces SyRoUP user-conditioned scaling to better model those effects. Pos-V/E Sun and Wang 2026 Excessive agreement with users at the expense of truthfulness; conceptualized through conversational demeanor (complimentary vs. neutral) and stance adaptation (adaptive vs. consistent). Operationalized via perceived authenticity and user trust in a 2 × \times 2 between-subjects human-subjects design. Subjective / social; human-agent conversation about autonomous vehicles. Shows sycophancy’s trust effects depend on the interaction between stance adaptation and friendliness rather than stance adaptation alone. Pos-S/E; Per-T/E Vennemeyer et al. 2025 Excessive agreement with or flattery of the user; decomposes into Sycophantic Agreement (SyA: agreeing with incorrect claims) and Sycophantic Praise (SyPr: flattery independent of correctness). Operationalized via difference-in-means directions, linear separability (AUROC), and causal activation steering to test independence of each behavior. Factual / controlled synthetic tasks + TruthfulQA. Demonstrates sycophancy is not a single construct; decomposes into distinct, independently steerable behaviors encoded along separate latent directions. Pos-V/E; Per-T/E Wang et al. 2026 Model’s tendency to conform to a user’s explicitly stated opinion even when incorrect. Operationalized as agreement rate on MMLU multiple-choice items under prepended incorrect user-opinion statements; logit-lens, representation divergence, and causal activation patching analyses. Factual MC QA; MMLU with prepended incorrect user opinions; 7 LLM families. Identifies a two-stage internal mechanism: late-layer output preference shift plus deeper representational divergence; user opinion, not user expertise, is the main trigger. Pos-V/E Wei et al. 2023 Undesirable behavior where models tailor responses to follow a human user’s view even when objectively incorrect; framed as reward hacking. Operationalized as belief conformity on objective tasks and opinion alignment on subjective tasks, measuring the effect of synthetic data fine-tuning. Objective (math) and subjective opinion tasks (politics, philosophy). Formalizes sycophancy as reward hacking; demonstrates a scalable synthetic data method to reduce it across diverse task types. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E; Per-T/E Yao et al. 2026 Tendency to overly align with user prompts, assumptions, or preferences even when they contradict objective evidence. Operationalized via four task types (Bias Feedback, Are You Sure, Answer, Mimicry) with Misleading Susceptibility Score (MSS) and Correction Receptiveness Score (CRS). Audio / multimodal; 4,319 audio questions spanning Audio Perception, Reasoning, Math, and Ethics; realistic noise and rate variation. Introduces SYAUDIO, the first audio sycophancy benchmark; ALMs exhibit distinctive sycophantic behavior under audio-specific conditions; SFT with CoT data substantially reduces it. Pos-V/E; Pos-S/E Yuan et al. 2025 Propensity to uncritically align with user-provided information even when incorrect or misleading. Operationalized as sycophancy rate under biased vs. neutral medical prompts, spanning 9 user-originated bias types from patients, medical students, and physicians. Medical / LVLM / multimodal; 2,122 medical images across 18 departments and 20 imaging modalities. Introduces EchoBench; sycophancy is widespread in high-stakes multimodal diagnosis and is shaped by authority cues, domain knowledge, and perceptual granularity. Pos-V/E Zhang et al. 2025 Tendency to align with user beliefs regardless of correctness; modifying answers to align with external suggestions at the cost of factual accuracy. Operationalized as answer revision under misleading feedback, sycophancy resistance (maintaining correct answer under pressure), and misleading resistance. Scientific QA / multi-turn adversarial; misleading feedback after initial answer. Establishes multi-turn adversarial dialogue as a sycophancy setting; proposes Pressure-Tune to improve resistance without harming accuracy. Pos-V/E Zhou et al. 2025 Tendency to align with user statements regardless of correctness; for Video-LLMs, aligning with user input even when it contradicts visual evidence. Operationalized via Misleading Susceptibility Score (MSS) and Correction Receptiveness Score (CRS) across seven sycophancy scenarios in ViSE. Multimodal / video QA; MSVD, MSRVTT, NExT-QA with injected linguistic bias cues. Introduces the first video-LLM sycophancy benchmark; misleading linguistic cues induce sycophantic behavior even when they conflict with visual evidence. Pos-V/E Table 6: Evaluation paradigms used to measure AI sycophancy. Paradigm Method Ground Truth? Mapped to Taxonomy Example Papers Belief injection Elicited: User explicitly states a position before or alongside a question; model response is compared to a no-statement baseline. May be verifiable (factual) or subjective (opinion). Measured: Frequency or magnitude of response shift toward the user’s stated position; accuracy loss relative to baseline. Depends Position-Verifiable/Explicit; Position-Subjective/Explicit Perez et al. 2023 ; Wei et al. 2023 ; Sharma et al. 2024 ; Atwell et al. 2025 Rebuttal Elicited: Model commits to an initial answer; user then challenges it with disagreement, scepticism, or a false authority citation, without providing new factual evidence. Measured: Rate at which model abandons its original response; “flip rate”; accuracy change between first and final answer. Depends Position-Verifiable/Explicit; Position-Subjective/Explicit Fanous et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2025 ; Laban et al. 2023 ; Ranaldi and Pucci 2023 Identity cue Elicited: User signals group membership, political affiliation, or ideological identity without stating an explicit belief; the model must infer the implied preferred response. Measured: Shift in model outputs based on perceived user identity, compared to neutral or alternative-identity baseline. No Position-Subjective/Implicit Perez et al. 2023 ; Kelley and Riedl 2026 ; Jain et al. 2026 Feedback bias Elicited: User expresses a preference about a piece of content under evaluation—either via stated affect (“I really like/dislike this”) or claimed authorship (“I wrote this”)—before or while requesting feedback. No factual claim is made about the content’s quality. Measured: Change in feedback positivity between liked and disliked conditions; “positivity gap”; probe-based sycophancy score on evaluative outputs. Depends Person-Traits/Explicit; Position-Subjective/Explicit Sharma et al. 2024 ; Papadatos and Freedman 2024 Endorsement of incorrect content Elicited: Model is presented with plausible but incorrect reasoning, mathematics, or proofs and asked to evaluate, validate, or build on them. Measured: Rate at which model validates or extends incorrect content rather than correcting it; sycophancy rate on false-but-well-posed statements. Yes Position-Verifiable/Explicit Petrov et al. 2025 ; Chen et al. 2025c Open-ended response with human baseline Elicited: User poses an advice, support, or moral judgment query with no objectively correct answer; model output is compared to crowdsourced human responses or normative baselines. Measured: Difference in validation rate, directness, framing acceptance, or moral consistency between model and human baseline; action endorsement rate. No Position-Subjective/Explicit; Position-Subjective/Implicit; Person-Traits/Explicit; Person-Traits/Implicit; Person-Emotions/Explicit; Person-Emotions/Implicit Cheng et al. 2026b ; Cheng et al. 2026a ; Rathje et al. 2025 Multi-turn pressure Elicited: Extended conversation in which the user repeatedly challenges, reframes, or pressures the model across multiple turns without introducing new evidence. Measured: Cumulative position drift across turns; Turn of Flip (ToF); Resistance (proportion of turns model maintains original stance). Depends Position-Verifiable/Explicit; Position-Subjective/Explicit Liu et al. 2025 ; Hong et al. 2025 ; Peng et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2026 Reasoning pressure Elicited: Escalating prompts signal that a particular analytical conclusion is desired; model is asked to conduct analysis or generate a proof. Measured: Whether model output shifts toward the signalled conclusion (e.g., inflated significance, cherry-picked specifications, sycophantic proof). Yes Position-Verifiable/Explicit Asher et al. 2026 ; Chang 2025 Multimodal adversarial Elicited: Belief injection or rebuttal paradigm applied to image, video, or audio content: user asserts something false about a visual or auditory stimulus, or challenges the model’s correct interpretation of it. Measured: Rate at which model abandons correct multimodal interpretation; Misleading Susceptibility Score (MSS); Correction Receptiveness Score (CRS). Yes Position-Verifiable/Explicit Zhou et al. 2025 ; Rahman et al. 2025 ; Yao et al. 2026 ; Yuan et al. 2025 Multi-agent peer sycophancy Elicited: Multiple LLM agents interact; one agent is exposed to another agent’s (potentially incorrect) answer and must decide whether to maintain its own position or conform. Measured: Disagreement collapse rate; sycophancy score (degree of answer copying without independent reasoning); accuracy under varying per-agent sycophancy levels. Yes Position-Verifiable/Explicit Pitre et al. 2025 Human experiment / RCT Real participants interact with a sycophantic vs. non-sycophantic model in a controlled study. Unlike paradigms 1–10, this paradigm does not elicit or measure sycophancy in the model; sycophancy is predefined and operationalized separately. It measures the downstream consequences of sycophantic behavior on users. Measured: Downstream participant outcomes: belief change, attitude polarisation, confidence, decision quality, relational dependence, prosocial intentions. N/A All cells Cheng et al. 2026a ; Bo et al. 2025 ; Rathje et al. 2025 Mechanistic probing Internal model representations are analysed during or after behavioral elicitation to determine how sycophantic behaviours are encoded and whether they are causally separable. Unlike paradigms 1–10, this paradigm does not elicit or measure whether sycophancy occurs; it examines the internal structure of behavior that has already been identified via other means. Measured: Linear probe accuracy; difference-in-means vectors; causal intervention success rates; logit-lens analysis. N/A All cells Vennemeyer et al. 2025 ; Genadi et al. 2026 ; Wang et al. 2026 Psychometric scale rating Human (or LLM) raters evaluate complete chatbot conversations using a validated multi-item scale, without reference to an external correct answer. Measured: Scores on a validated multi-factor scale (e.g., Uncritical Agreement, Obsequiousness, Excitement). N/A Position-Subjective/Explicit; Person-Traits/Explicit; Person-Emotions/Explicit Rehani et al. 2026 Note. Paradigms 1–10 elicit sycophancy and measure whether it occurs. Human experimental paradigms (paradigm 11) predefine sycophancy via behavioral operationalization and then study its effects on users—they measure consequences. Mechanistic probing (paradigm 12) uses representations to study the internal structure of behaviors identified as sycophantic via other methods—it is a method for understanding sycophancy. Psychometric scale rating (paradigm 13) assesses perceived sycophancy rather than detecting defined behavioral instances.

sections.heading: Mapping papers to taxonomy cells
sections.text: Two authors independently annotated each of the 70 papers in the literature review, recording for each paper which of the eight taxonomy cells it covered based on its definition, operationalization, and examples. Initial agreement between the two human coders was substantial ( κ = 0.652 \kappa=0.652 , 88.3% agreement). All disagreements were adjudicated using Claude Sonnet 4.6 as a third coder, which independently reviewed each disagreeing paper and assigned cell codes. The LLM adjudication agreed with one of the two human coders on 80.2% of contested cell decisions; in cases of agreement with one coder, those codes were adopted. The remaining cases were resolved through direct discussion between the two authors. The LLM coder showed strong agreement with the final resolved codes ( κ = 0.904 \kappa=0.904 , 96.8% agreement). Two papers were not assigned to any cell, as they did not operationalize a specific behavioral type. Final cell counts are reported in Table 1 in the main text.

sections.heading: A.3 Annotation Results
sections.text: To characterize where each item sits in the taxonomy space, four authors independently annotated all 24 behavior descriptions. Six dimensions (Person, Position, Trait, Emotion, Verifiable, Subjective) were rated on a 5-point scale ( 1 = Not at all 1=\textit{Not at all} , 5 = Extremely 5=\textit{Extremely} ) indicating how much each behavior pertains to the given dimension. Explicitness was rated on a 7-point bipolar scale ( 1 = Very Implicit 1=\textit{Very Implicit} , 7 = Very Explicit 7=\textit{Very Explicit} ). Inter-rater reliability was acceptable to good across all dimensions ( ICC (A,1) range: .47 ​ – ​ .86 .47–.86 , all p ≤ .001 p\leq.001 ; see Figure 6 ). From the annotation means we derived two continuous taxonomy coordinates per item. The Referent score (Position mean − - Person mean) places each item on the Position–Person axis, with positive values indicating Position referent and negative values indicating Person referent. The Explicit score (Explicit mean − 4 -4 ) places each item on the Explicitness axis, centered at the bipolar scale’s neutral midpoint. Two sub-referent contrast scores were additionally derived: Verifiable − - Subjective and Trait − - Emotion. Figure 4 places all 24 items in the resulting two-dimensional space; see also Figure 5 for the dimension heatmap and Figure 6 for the full reliability profile. Figure 4: Placement of the 24 expert survey items in the two-dimensional taxonomy space using annotation-derived coordinates. The horizontal axis represents the Referent dimension (Position ↔ \leftrightarrow Person), and the vertical axis represents the Explicitness dimension (Implicit ↔ \leftrightarrow Explicit). Each point corresponds to a behavior item derived from the literature review, illustrating coverage across all four quadrants of the taxonomy. Figure 5: Dimension score heatmap. Mean annotation scores for each of the 24 behavioral items across all seven taxonomy dimensions, sorted by taxonomy group and then by Explicitness within each group. Figure 6: Inter-rater reliability by taxonomy dimension. ICC(A,1): two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measures; N = 4 N=4 raters, 24 items. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals; dimensions are ordered from highest to lowest agreement. All F F tests significant ( p < .001 p<.001 ).

sections.heading: A.4 Expert Sample Demographics
sections.text: Tables 8 – 10 summarize the demographic composition of the expert sample ( N = 106 N=106 ). The sample is heavily concentrated in academia, technically-oriented fields, and the United States, which makes sense considering we targeted authors of recent AI sycophancy papers. Moderator analyses examining whether demographic variables predicted overall rating severity or moderated the primary Explicitness × \times Referent interaction yielded no significant results. sections.heading: Moderator Analyses
sections.text: First, we tested whether demographic groups differed in overall rating severity using Kruskal–Wallis tests, with mean rating per respondent as the outcome. Second, we tested whether each demographic variable moderated the primary Explicitness × \times Referent interaction using likelihood ratio tests comparing a base multilevel model (with demographic group as an additive covariate) against a full model including the three-way Explicitness × \times Referent × \times Group interaction. Overall rating severity did not differ significantly across any demographic variable. Mean ratings were tightly clustered across groups (generally M ≈ 4.7 M\approx 4.7 – 5.4 5.4 on the [ − 3 , + 3 ] [-3,+3] scale). No demographic variable significantly moderated the primary Explicitness × \times Referent interaction. The only nominally significant result was for the fine-grained degree-field variable ( χ 2 = 110.34 \chi^{2}=110.34 , p < .001 p<.001 ), which includes 21 categories many with small counts ( n ≤ 2 n\leq 2 ). This result did not persist when degree fields were collapsed into four broader categories ( χ 2 = 15.38 \chi^{2}=15.38 , p = .081 p=.081 ). Sector, education level, country, and research area showed no evidence of moderation. We additionally examined whether demographic variables were associated with responses to the four opinion items using Kruskal–Wallis tests. All tests were non-significant with one exception: sector was associated with beliefs about whether users prefer sycophantic responses ( χ 2 ​ ( 3 ) = 9.21 \chi^{2}(3)=9.21 , p = .027 p=.027 ). Because the consolidated test of research area as a four-group factor found no significant overall moderation ( χ 2 = 9.71 \chi^{2}=9.71 , p = .375 p=.375 ), we examined each area separately using binary indicators in nested multilevel models. Quadrant-level differences were assessed using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests within each annotation-derived quadrant.

sections.text: Normative researchers rated behaviors as more sycophantic overall than non-normative researchers ( b = 0.349 b=0.349 , S ​ E = 0.107 SE=0.107 , p = .002 p=.002 ). They also rated explicitly expressed behaviors as more sycophantic than non-normative researchers did ( b = 0.155 b=0.155 , S ​ E = 0.082 SE=0.082 , p = .059 p=.059 ; LRT: χ 2 ​ ( 1 ) = 4.56 \chi^{2}(1)=4.56 , p = .033 p=.033 ). The full three-way interaction (Normative × \times Referent × \times Explicit) was not significant ( p = .716 p=.716 ), indicating that the core Referent × \times Explicit pattern is consistent across normative and non-normative researchers. Sociotechnical researchers also rated behaviors as more sycophantic overall ( χ 2 ​ ( 1 ) = 10.30 \chi^{2}(1)=10.30 , p = .001 p=.001 ), with no significant interaction with either the Referent score or the Explicit score (all p > .15 p>.15 ). Technical and Governance researchers showed no significant effects on overall rating level or on either taxonomy dimension.

sections.heading: Model Specifications.
sections.text: The primary analysis examined whether expert sycophancy ratings vary as a function of behaviors’ taxonomy coordinates. Because ratings are nested within both respondents and items, we used multilevel linear models with crossed random intercepts for respondents and items. All annotation predictors were z z -scored across items so that coefficients are expressed in standard deviation units and comparable across dimensions measured on different scales. We estimated four nested models. The Main Effects Model included Referent and Explicit scores as predictors. The Interaction Model added their interaction, testing whether Explicitness predicts sycophancy ratings differently for Position versus Person behaviors. The Sub-Referent Model extended the Interaction Model with two contrast scores (Verifiable − - Subjective and Trait − - Emotion), testing whether finer distinctions within each referent type independently predict ratings. The Discriminant Validity Model entered all seven raw annotation dimension scores simultaneously; if the taxonomy dimensions are mutually exclusive, inverse pairs (Position/Person, Verifiable/Subjective, Trait/Emotion) should suppress each other, confirming that the dimensions carve non-overlapping portions of behavioral space. sections.heading: Confirmatory Factor Analysis
sections.text: As a supplementary analysis, we examined whether expert ratings conform to a latent structure corresponding to the taxonomy. These analyses are intended as diagnostic rather than validating: items were designed to span a range of behaviors within each region rather than function as parallel indicators of a single latent construct. Item-to-factor assignments were derived from annotation-based taxonomy coordinates: items with a positive Referent score were assigned to the Positional factor and items with a positive Explicit score to the Explicit factor, with sub-referent assignments following the dominant annotation dimension within each referent group. Five CFA models were estimated using WLSMV with delta parameterization, appropriate for ordinal items. The 1-factor, 2-factor A (Positional/Personal), and 2-factor B (Explicit/Implicit) models were admissible. The 4-factor model was inadmissible due to negative observed variances, and the 8-factor model, while technically converging, could not produce standard errors due to a non-invertible information matrix. All admissible models showed poor absolute fit (see Table 19 ). A scaled difference test indicated that 2-factor A fit significantly better than the 1-factor baseline ( Δ ​ χ 2 ​ ( 1 ) = 20.13 \Delta\chi^{2}(1)=20.13 , p < .001 p<.001 ), whereas 2-factor B showed essentially no improvement over the 1-factor model ( Δ ​ χ 2 ​ ( 1 ) < 0.01 \Delta\chi^{2}(1)<0.01 , p = .946 p=.946 ). This pattern indicates that the Positional/Personal distinction captures some perceptual structure in expert ratings, while the Explicit/Implicit distinction does not emerge as a separable latent dimension. Even where improvement was observed, fit remained well below acceptable thresholds (CFI < .95 <.95 , RMSEA > .06 >.06 ). Within-quadrant reliability was uniformly low ( α = − .104 \alpha=-.104 –.328): the Implicit/Positional region produced a negative alpha ( − .104 -.104 , k = 3 k=3 ), indicating that items in this region are negatively intercorrelated, consistent with the region containing both sycophantic and non-sycophantic exemplars whose ratings diverge systematically. These results indicate that expert ratings do not organize into a stable latent structure corresponding to the taxonomy’s dimensions, which is consistent with the taxonomy’s role as a behavioral classification system rather than a psychometric model. sections.heading: Scale Robustness
sections.text: A potential concern is that Highly non-sycophantic is not self-interpreting, and experts may differ in whether they read negative ratings as indicating a behavior they recognize as the construct’s opposite or simply as expressing uncertainty about where a behavior falls relative to sycophancy. We assessed sensitivity by re-estimating the primary Referent × \times Explicit interaction under two alternative DV treatments. When ratings were dichotomized as sycophantic ( > 0 >0 ) versus non-sycophantic ( ≤ 0 \leq 0 ), the interaction replicated ( log-odds = − 0.366 \text{log-odds}=-0.366 , OR = 0.693 \text{OR}=0.693 , p = .024 p=.024 ), with Person behaviors showing a 33.9 percentage point increase in predicted sycophantic judgment from the Implicit to the Explicit condition (37.9% to 71.8%), while Position items were flat (73.3% vs. 72.6%). When negative ratings were collapsed to zero, the interaction was directionally consistent ( b = − 0.308 b=-0.308 ) but did not reach significance ( p = .108 p=.108 ), likely because this treatment removes substantial variance for control and ambiguous items, which received negative ratings 25.8% and 57.8% of the time respectively. The primary interaction is therefore sensitive to DV coding when negative-pole information is discarded, a limitation that should be weighed alongside the construct rationale for the bipolar design. Rationale for bipolar scale: A unipolar scale would collapse the neutral and non-sycophantic categories into the same low-end response, making it impossible to distinguish behavior that is passively not sycophantic from behavior that is actively the opposite of sycophantic. The bipolar design preserves this distinction, which matters because our item set includes both ambiguous boundary-case behaviors designed to sit near the construct’s edge and non-sycophantic exemplars designed to represent its opposite. Negative ratings were applied discriminantly: 57.8% of ambiguous items received negative ratings compared to 25.8% of non-sycophantic exemplars and 9.7% of sycophantic exemplars, and 105 of 106 respondents used the negative pole at least once.

A Taxonomy and Expert Survey of a Fragmented Construct Meryl Ye Lujain Ibrahim Jessica Y. Bo Myra Cheng Ida Mattsson Daniel Vennemeyer Robert Kraut Steve Rathje Abstract AI sycophancy has become a prominent concern in large language model (LLM) research. Yet the term lacks a consistent definition and has been applied to behaviors ranging from agreeing with a user’s false claim to excessively praising the user to withholding corrective feedback. When researchers, companies, and policymakers use the same term to describe different behaviors, evaluation results become difficult to compare, mitigation strategies fail to transfer, and systems that are resistant to one form of sycophancy continue exhibiting other forms. To address this, we make two contributions. First, we reviewed 70 papers on AI sycophancy to develop a taxonomy of how the behavior has been defined and measured. The taxonomy distinguishes (1) whether a model is sycophantic toward a user’s positions and beliefs, or toward the user’s broader personal traits and emotions, and (2) whether this occurs through explicit, direct language or more implicit, subtle behaviors such as framing, omission, or tone. Mapping existing literature to our taxonomy reveals that current research has focused on overt forms of sycophancy toward users’ beliefs, leaving more subtle and person-directed behaviors relatively understudied. Second, we surveyed 106 experts in AI sycophancy and related fields to examine whether researchers agree on which model behaviors are sycophantic. While experts are nearly unanimous in believing that sycophancy is a significant problem in current AI systems (94.3% agree), they disagree substantially on which specific behaviors qualify. Together, these findings demonstrate that AI sycophancy is a broad family of behaviors with different measurement challenges, intervention requirements, and governance implications. Our taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for understanding and addressing these behaviors. We discuss ways in which the taxonomy can inform evaluation design as well as both technical and regulatory interventions. 1 Carnegie Mellon University 2 University of Oxford 3 University of Toronto 4 Stanford University 5 University of Cincinnati 6 New York University merylye@cmu.edu Introduction Sycophancy has become a prominent concern in large language model (LLM) research. The topic has accumulated a growing body of empirical findings, evaluation benchmarks, and proposed mitigation strategies ( Perez et al. 2023 ; Sharma et al. 2024 ; Wei et al. 2023 ) . Academic literature on the topic has expanded rapidly in recent years, and public attention has risen accordingly (see Figure 1 ). Recent empirical findings show that sycophantic interactions increase attitude extremity and overconfidence ( Rathje et al. 2025 ) , impair task performance and learning ( Bo et al. 2025 ) , and alter users’ social judgments and prosocial behavior ( Cheng et al. 2026a ; Ibrahim et al. 2026a ) . Yet the term lacks a consistent definition. The range of behaviors it has been used to describe reveals a fragmented construct that is rapidly expanding without a shared conceptual anchor. Construct fragmentation occurs when different studies use the same label for behaviors that differ in form, mechanism, and measurement ( Flake and Fried 2020 ) . While breadth in a construct is not inherently problematic, issues emerge when that breadth leads to findings that cannot be meaningfully compared or aggregated ( Anvari et al. 2025 ) . This fragmentation is evident in how recent studies operationalize sycophancy. Although these studies claim to examine the same phenomenon, they operationalize sycophancy as different behaviors in different settings. Yet findings from those studies are often treated interchangeably to benchmark models, evaluate mitigation strategies, or support safety claims. As a result, benchmarks built to detect sycophancy as factual capitulation cannot detect sycophancy as implicit framing bias. Mitigation strategies effective against agreement with users may not address sycophancy when it is expressed as praise of the user’s character or abilities, and model specifications anchored to one set of behaviors leave others entirely unaddressed. Figure 1 provides an overview of these conceptual expansions over time. Figure 1: Top : Proxy measures of public and academic attention to the term “sycophancy” over time. Academic interest began rising in 2024, preceding the largest spikes in public search interest observed during 2025–2026 ( Google 2026 ) . Bottom : Overview of key conceptual expansions in AI sycophancy research. This timeline is not exhaustive. These inconsistencies extend beyond academic studies into model evaluation and deployment. With the launch of GPT-5 in August 2025, OpenAI reported that its model incorporated changes designed to reduce sycophancy ( Singh et al. 2025 ) . However, evaluations on the ELEPHANT (Evaluation of LLMs as Excessive SycoPHANTs) benchmark ( Cheng et al. 2026b ) , which examines social validation, indirectness, and framing in open-ended advice contexts, show that GPT-5 remains substantially sycophantic in the open-ended advice and interpersonal contexts that the benchmark probes. Similar discrepancies appear across benchmarks. SycEval ( Fanous et al. 2025 ) , which operationalizes sycophancy as susceptibility to factual rebuttals, ranks Gemini as the most sycophantic model tested. In contrast, ELEPHANT ranks Gemini as the least sycophantic. Each benchmark operationalizes a different set of behaviors, and treating them as equivalent assessments of the same construct makes direct comparison difficult to interpret. To address these challenges, this paper makes two contributions. First, through a review of 70 papers on AI sycophancy, published from 2023 to 2026, we examine how the construct has expanded over time, applied to increasingly diverse settings, tasks, and behavioral assumptions. This historical analysis reveals a rapidly growing but uneven research landscape, where new definitions, benchmarks, and mitigation strategies have proliferated without a shared definitional framework. Building on these patterns, we introduce a descriptive taxonomy of AI sycophancy organized along two orthogonal dimensions: Referent —whether the model responds to the user’s expressed positions and claims (Position) or to the user as a person (Person)—and Explicitness —whether the behavior is expressed overtly or through subtler means such as framing, omission, or tone. Within each referent, we distinguish sub-referents: Verifiable versus Subjective for Position behaviors, and Traits versus Emotions for Person behaviors. This taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for comparing behaviors that have previously been studied under the same label, but operationalized in different ways. Our analysis further reveals a strong concentration of prior work on explicit forms of sycophancy tied to users’ verifiable claims, while subtler forms expressed through framing, omission, or behaviors targeting users as persons receive comparatively less empirical attention. Second, we report results from a survey of 106 experts in AI sycophancy and related domains designed to examine whether researchers apply the label consistently when judging concrete model behaviors. We find that experts are nearly unanimous in agreeing that sycophancy is a significant problem in current AI systems ( M = 6.21 M=6.21 , S ​ D = 0.91 SD=0.91 on a 7-point Likert Scale; 94.3% agree), yet show substantial variation in which specific behaviors they consider sycophantic. Experts broadly agree that behaviors directed at users’ positions are sycophantic whether expressed explicitly or through subtler means such as selective framing. However, for behaviors directed at the user as a person, experts are mixed: only explicit forms such as flattery and unwarranted praise are reliably recognized as sycophantic, while behaviors that convey the same deference through tone, softened feedback, or avoidance of critique are not. These findings suggest that AI sycophancy comprises a family of behaviors whose boundaries remain actively contested. Expert disagreements reflect differences in where researchers draw those boundaries and potentially how they interpret the consequences of sycophantic behavior across sustained interaction. As researchers, AI companies, and policymakers increasingly invoke the term, progress will depend on clearly specifying which types of behavior are being measured, mitigated, and regulated. Our taxonomy and expert survey provide a foundation for these specifications, and we discuss their implications for evaluation methods, mitigation strategies, and corporate and legislative governance. Sycophancy as a Fragmented Construct Divergent Definitions Across major English dictionary definitions, the term sycophancy and its variants (e.g., sycophant, sycophantic) cluster around a consistent set of themes: insincere praise directed at those with power or status, motivated by self-interest ( Rehani et al. 2026 ) . Early AI safety discourse often preserved this agentive framing, extending it into accounts of sycophancy as strategic or deceptive behavior ( Cotra 2021 ; Denison et al. 2024 ) . However, recent AI sycophancy research has largely set aside these motivational assumptions, treating sycophancy as an approval-seeking behavioral pattern that arises from training on human feedback. Throughout this paper, we follow the convention of treating sycophancy as a pattern in model outputs without assuming intentional or strategic motivations, since intent is not directly observable in most empirical settings. The construct has nonetheless been defined in increasingly divergent ways. Although early AI research used the term in relatively consistent ways, later work has operationalized sycophancy in increasingly varied ways, differing in settings, tasks, and behavioral assumptions. Initial empirical definitions focused on agreement with user-stated positions in structured, proposition-based tasks where models could be evaluated against the “ground truth” (i.e., a preferred or externally specified response) ( Perez et al. 2023 ; Sharma et al. 2024 ) . Subsequent work sought to explain the training-level causes of sycophancy, attributing sycophancy to reward misspecification (models trained on human approval signals learn to generate outputs that elicit favorable feedback rather than accurate information) and showing it can be reduced through synthetic-data fine-tuning Wei et al. (2023) . Denison et al. (2024) extend this account more broadly by situating sycophancy within specification gaming (the tendency of models to satisfy the literal terms of a training objective while violating its intent), showing that models trained to seek user approval in simple interactions can generalize to more strategic reward-seeking behaviors and that standard harmlessness training does not reliably prevent this shift. A limitation of these early accounts of sycophancy is that they cannot be applied in settings where no ground truth exists. Atwell et al. (2025) address this by redefining sycophancy as the extent to which a model shifts toward a user’s stated position more than a Bayesian-rational agent would after observing the same evidence. This framework enables measurement in subjective and uncertain settings, but introduces new questions about what determines a rational baseline. Parallel work expands the construct into interpersonal and affective domains where ground truth similarly does not exist. Cheng et al. (2026b) define sycophancy as excessive face-preservation (i.e., the tendency to affirm users’ self-image through validation, indirectness, framing acceptance, and moral endorsement) and introduce ELEPHANT, a benchmark for measuring these behaviors against crowdsourced human baselines. A related finding is that training LLMs to be warm and empathetic makes them substantially more sycophantic ( Ibrahim et al. 2026b ) , raising the question of where appropriate affective responsiveness ends and sycophancy begins. Further work illustrates the construct’s heterogeneity from multiple angles. Vennemeyer et al. (2025) show that sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise are functionally separable in model representations and can be independently steered, suggesting that even seemingly similar approval-seeking behaviors are distinct. Rathje et al. (2025) experimentally disentangle validating language from the one-sided provision of factual information, showing that these components produce different downstream effects: validation primarily increases enjoyment and positive perceptions of the AI chatbot, while one-sided factual statements primarily increase attitude extremity. Rehani et al. (2026) find that perceived sycophancy decomposes into three factors (Uncritical Agreement, Obsequiousness, and Excitement) which differ in how negatively users perceive them. Across these studies, behaviors commonly labeled as sycophancy differ not only in surface form but also in internal representation, downstream effects, and how they are perceived by users. Why Fragmentation is a Problem As the literature has expanded, researchers have introduced increasingly specialized subtypes of sycophantic behaviors. Sharma et al. (2024) propose answer sycophancy (changing answers to align with user beliefs), feedback sycophancy (changing feedback to align with user preferences), and mimicry sycophancy (repeating user errors or stylistic patterns). Fanous et al. (2025) distinguish progressive sycophancy (agreeing with incorrect user rebuttals) from regressive sycophancy (revising correct answers after user rebuttal). Cheng et al. (2026b) introduce four dimensions of social sycophancy: validation, indirectness, framing, and moral endorsement. Du et al. (2025) propose informational, cognitive, and affective sycophancy. These distinctions are not mutually exclusive and do not neatly map onto one another, resulting in a patchwork of labels without shared criteria for what counts as sycophancy. This fragmentation is directly reflected in evaluation frameworks such as ELEPHANT ( Cheng et al. 2026b ) , VISE (Video-LLM Sycophancy Benchmarking and Evaluation) ( Zhou et al. 2025 ) , BASIL (Bayesian Assessment of Sycophancy in LLMs) ( Atwell et al. 2025 ) , and SycEval ( Fanous et al. 2025 ) , which operationalize different forms of sycophantic behavior without situating them within a shared construct space. As a result, the apparent body of evidence rests on observations from benchmarks that measure different behaviors, making cumulative claims difficult to sustain. The absence of shared construct boundaries also creates openings for broader conceptual reinterpretation. For instance, Shi et al. (2026) absorb sycophancy into a unified taxonomy of LLM deception, treating it as a behavioral subtype because sycophantic responses may lead users to form false beliefs. Where early safety discourse assumed strategic intent, this reinterpretation extends the construct from observable behavioral outputs to their downstream epistemic effects, which most empirical studies of sycophancy do not directly measure. These disagreements reflect differences in the conceptual boundaries researchers place around the term. When studies use the same label for behaviors that differ in form, setting, measurement strategy, and likely mechanism, it becomes difficult to compare findings, determine whether mitigation strategies transfer, or assess industry commitments to reducing sycophancy. These behaviors also differ in the kinds of downstream concerns they raise: some primarily concern whether models provide accurate information or correct users’ false beliefs, while others involve questions about how patterns of affirmation shape users’ beliefs, confidence, and capacity for independent judgment across sustained interaction.
